title: SR&ED Claim Filing Deadline with the CRA | Canada FAQ
description: What is the deadline for filing an SR&ED claim in Canada? Read our FAQ on the strict 18-month CRA reporting deadline after your corporate tax year-end.
summary: The SR&ED claim filing deadline in Canada requires corporations to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 within 12 months after the T2 filing-due date, which is generally 18 months after the end of the taxation year. Sole proprietors have until June 15 of the second following year. The CRA cannot waive or extend this deadline, and late claims are permanently barred.

This report delivers a technical audit and statutory reference analysis of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program, federal and provincial/territorial research and development (R&D) tax credits, administrative procedures, and governing jurisprudence in Canada as of November 2026.

Between December 2024 and October 2026, Canada enacted the most comprehensive structural overhaul of its federal and provincial R&D tax incentive landscape since the 2012 federal budget reforms. Following the release of the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) on December 16, 2024, and the tabling of Federal Budget 2025 on November 4, 2025, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Applying retroactively to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000—raising the maximum annual cash refund on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Simultaneously, Bill C-15 broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000), granted Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) an annual election to use the gross revenue phase-out formula in lieu of taxable capital, and reinstated the eligibility of capital expenditures and capital equipment lease costs incurred on or after December 16, 2024.

Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA introduced an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process that provides up-front technical eligibility determinations within an eight-week service standard and accelerates post-filing expenditure reviews to 90 calendar days. Across the provinces, Quebec replaced its entire legacy multi-credit R&D framework for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, with the consolidated, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC; also designated by Revenu Québec as the tax credit for R&D, innovation and pre-commercialization) at rates of 30% and 20%; British Columbia Budget 2026 made the 10% BC SR&ED tax credit permanent and harmonized its $6,000,000 refundable expenditure limit and public corporation eligibility with federal Bill C-15; and Saskatchewan doubled its 10% refundable CCPC expenditure limit from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 for qualifying expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024. By contrast, Ontario retained its separate $3,000,000 expenditure limit and strict CCPC-only restriction for the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC).
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Incentive Statutory Structure

Canada's federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program is jointly administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which oversees technical eligibility reviews, financial audits, and tax credit assessments, and the Department of Finance Canada, which establishes legislative policy under the federal Income Tax Act (the "Act" or "ITA") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (the "Regulations" or "ITR"). Unlike discretionary innovation grants, the SR&ED program is a statutory tax entitlement: any taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada that performs eligible SR&ED work and incurs qualifying expenditures in accordance with the Act is entitled to claim two distinct, sequential tax benefits.

The first statutory benefit is the Section 37 Income Deduction Pool. Pursuant to subsection 37(1) of the Act, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may accumulate allowable current SR&ED expenditures—and, for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, allowable capital SR&ED expenditures—incurred in Canada within a dedicated expenditure pool and deduct any portion of that pool in computing net business income for tax purposes in the current taxation year. Claiming a deduction from the Section 37 pool in a given year is optional; any positive undeducted balance in the pool does not expire and may be carried forward indefinitely to reduce taxable business income in future taxation years. However, if the taxpayer undergoes a "loss restriction event" (an acquisition of control of a corporation or a change in majority-interest beneficiary of a trust), subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h) deem a taxation year-end and restrict the carryforward of pre-acquisition undeducted SR&ED pool balances unless the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and then only to the extent of income from that same or a similar business. Partnerships are subject to a distinct restriction: because a partnership is not a separate taxpayer and cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance to a subsequent fiscal period, the entire Section 37 pool balance must be deducted in computing the partnership's net income or loss for the fiscal period in which the expenditures were incurred, and limited partners are prohibited from deducting any partnership loss created or increased by the partnership's Section 37 SR&ED deduction.

The second statutory benefit is the Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC). Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the Act, a taxpayer earns an SR&ED ITC calculated as a statutory percentage (the 15% basic rate or the 35% enhanced rate) of its net "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. Under subsection 127(5), earned SR&ED ITCs may first be applied to reduce federal Part I income tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year. Any unused non-refundable ITC balance may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to offset federal Part I tax payable, subject to acquisition-of-control streaming restrictions under subsections 127(9.1) and 127(9.2). Where no federal Part I tax is payable (or where earned ITCs exceed Part I tax payable), section 127.1 of the Act permits eligible claimants—including qualifying CCPCs, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), individuals, and certain trusts—to receive all or a statutory percentage (100% or 40%) of their unused current-year ITCs as a direct cash refund. Any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash under section 127.1 is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable, thereby extinguishing that credit from the carryforward/carryback pool.

A fundamental statutory feedback mechanism links the Section 127 ITC back to the Section 37 deduction pool. Under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the Act, any SR&ED ITC claimed by a taxpayer in Year 1 (whether applied against Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund) reduces the taxpayer's Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in Year 2. If the reduction required under paragraph 37(1)(d) in Year 2 exceeds the available balance in the Section 37 pool (which commonly occurs when a claimant deducts 100% of its Section 37 pool in Year 1 and incurs fewer SR&ED expenditures in Year 2), the excess negative balance must be included directly in the taxpayer's taxable business income in Year 2 pursuant to paragraph 12(1)(t) of the Act. Consequently, SR&ED ITCs are effectively taxable in the following taxation year. The sole timing exception applies to partnerships: because a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance, any SR&ED ITC allocated to partners under subsection 127(8) reduces the partnership's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the same fiscal period in which the expenditure was incurred, unless an active (non-specified) partner elects to renounce reallocated ITCs originating from a specified member's share using Form T932.
1.2 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

Eligibility for both the Section 37 expenditure deduction and the Section 127 ITC is governed by the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Harmonized generally with the OECD Frascati Manual, subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". That systematic investigation or search must fall within one of four inclusive statutory categories—paragraphs 248(1)(a) through (d)—and must not fall within any of the seven excluded categories enumerated in paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k).

body.text: In corporate practice, paragraph 248(1)(c) (experimental development)—together with its commensurate paragraph 248(1)(d) support work—accounts for the overwhelming majority of Canadian SR&ED claims, spanning shop-floor manufacturing process improvements, custom software architecture, machine learning model training, biotechnology, and hardware prototyping. Support work listed in paragraph 248(1)(d) is never eligible as SR&ED on its own; it qualifies solely when it is commensurate with the needs of, and directly supports, underlying basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada. Furthermore, as the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (published August 13, 2021) explain, the dividing line between eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) (such as data collection or testing) and excluded work under paragraphs 248(1)(f) or (k) (routine testing or routine data collection) is determined by purpose. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically for the purpose of testing a scientific or technological hypothesis within an active SR&ED investigation, it qualifies as support work; if it is conducted for commercial quality control, regulatory compliance of an established commercial product, or routine business operations, it is excluded.
1.3 CRA's "Why and How" Eligibility Guidelines vs. Statutory Jurisprudence

On August 13, 2021, the CRA archived its former Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and issued the current Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives, which structure the administrative evaluation of subsection 248(1) around two core requirements: the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement.

The "Why" requirement mandates that work be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. According to the CRA's guidelines, this focuses on generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (explanatory theories, principles, or predictive models) rather than merely accumulating factual knowledge (standard observations or measurements). A claimant only seeks a scientific or technological advancement when it confronts a scientific or technological uncertainty—a situation where it is unknown or uncertain whether a desired objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, due to an insufficiency or limitation in the available scientific or technological knowledge base (which encompasses both the internal resources of the business and publicly available knowledge accessible to competent professionals in the field). Indicators of technological uncertainty in experimental development include situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, specifications exceed existing industry standards, interlocking system constraints prevent predictable solutions, parameters lie outside normal operating ranges, or too many interacting variables exist. Acquiring existing knowledge through employee training, hiring external consultants, purchasing proprietary technology, or circumventing an uncertainty via standard workarounds does not satisfy the "Why" requirement. Conversely, actual commercial or technical success is unnecessary: an experiment that fails to achieve its performance target but generates new conceptual knowledge by proving why a hypothesized technological approach does not work fully satisfies the "Why" requirement.

The "How" requirement mandates that the work be carried out by qualified individuals through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Under the CRA guidelines, a systematic investigation requires four sequential elements: (1) generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts as a starting point for resolving the uncertainty; (2) testing that idea or hypothesis by means of structured experiment or analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve as testing progresses); (3) developing logical conclusions based on the experimental or analytical findings; and (4) keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses. Crucially, as the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, the CRA's administrative "Why and How" framing did not amend subsection 248(1) of the Act or displace the binding five-question judicial test established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen.
1.4 The 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms: Bill C-69, FES 2024, Budget 2025, and Bill C-15

Between June 2024 and March 2026, a sequence of federal legislative enactments fundamentally altered the financial parameters of the SR&ED program. First, on June 20, 2024, Bill C-69 (Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1) received Royal Assent, amending the definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) of the Act. Bill C-69 clarified that bona fide loans with reasonable repayment terms obtained from public authorities in Canada do not constitute government assistance that reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures, provided the loan meets the definition of an "excluded loan" in subsection 12(11) of the Act. This relieving amendment applies retroactively to loans made after December 31, 2019 (effective January 1, 2020), allowing claimants with non-statute-barred taxation years who previously deducted such public loans as government assistance on Form T661 to file amended tax returns and recover lost ITCs.

Second, on December 16, 2024, the Department of Finance released the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024), announcing sweeping structural enhancements for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. FES 2024 initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000 (which would have yielded $1,575,000 in maximum annual refundable credits), widening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extending the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000), allowing CCPCs to elect into the gross revenue phase-out structure, and restoring capital expenditures and capital lease costs incurred on or after December 16, 2024.

Third, in Federal Budget 2025 (tabled November 4, 2025) and Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026), Parliament enacted all of the FES 2024 structural reforms while further increasing the annual expenditure limit from the previously announced $4,500,000 to $6,000,000, retroactive to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Although August 2025 draft legislative explanatory notes from the Department of Finance (ita-lir-0825-n-eng) still reflected the interim $4,500,000 FES figure in their commentary on subsection 127(10.6), the enacted text of Bill C-15 and the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (published October 7, 2026) confirm that the statutory expenditure limit for both CCPCs and ECPCs for all taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, is $6,000,000. The taxable capital phase-out range for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, was $10,000,000 to $50,000,000.

Finally, although the Department of Finance conducted stakeholder consultations in 2024 regarding a potential "patent box" intellectual property regime and an innovation flow-through share mechanism, neither proposal was included in Federal Budget 2025 or Bill C-15, and Budget 2025 provided no indication as to whether those two proposals have been deferred or abandoned. In their place, Parliament enacted immediate capital expensing incentives—referred to in Budget 2025 and tax practice as the "Productivity Super-Deduction" or "Productivity Mega Deduction"—which include 100% immediate expensing under Bill C-15 for qualifying purchases of patents (Class 44), data network infrastructure equipment (Class 46), and general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and systems software (Class 50) acquired on or after April 16, 2024, and available for use before January 1, 2027.

2.1 Rate Matrix and Refundability by Taxpayer Classification

The statutory rate at which a claimant earns federal SR&ED ITCs under section 127—and the percentage of unused credits that can be refunded in cash under section 127.1—varies according to both the legal classification of the claimant and whether the underlying expenditure is of a current or capital nature. Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (published October 7, 2026) and subsections 127(10.1) and 127.1(2.01) of the Act, seven distinct taxpayer categories govern federal SR&ED claims for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

body.text: Under the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026) and section 127.1 of the Act, the statutory refund rate for individuals (sole proprietorships), certain trusts, and eligible partnership allocations on the 15% basic ITC is 40% (yielding an effective 6% cash refund and a 9% non-refundable tax credit). Furthermore, because a partnership is not a corporation, subsection 127(8) restricts all SR&ED ITCs computed at the partnership level to the 15% basic rate, even if the partners are qualifying CCPCs; moreover, no SR&ED ITC may be allocated to a "specified member" of a partnership (such as a limited partner or passive general partner).
2.2 Definition and Criteria for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Historically, a Canadian-controlled private corporation that listed its shares on a public stock exchange immediately ceased to be a CCPC, forfeiting access to the 35% refundable ITC and dropping to the 15% non-refundable basic rate. To eliminate this disincentive for domestic public listings, Bill C-15 amended subsections 127(9), 127(10.1), 127(10.6), and 127.1(2.01) of the Act effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, extending the 35% refundable ITC up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit to any Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC).

Under subsection 127(9) of the Act, a corporation qualifies as an ECPC if it satisfies either of two statutory definitions throughout the taxation year. Under the first branch (Direct Public Corporation Test), the corporation must, throughout the taxation year: (1) be resident in Canada; (2) have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (as published by the Minister of Finance under section 262) or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation under subsection 89(1); and (3) not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatsoever (encompassing both de jure voting control and de facto control under subsection 256(5.1)) by one or more non-resident persons. Under the second branch (Corporate Subsidiary Test), a private Canadian-resident corporation also qualifies as an ECPC if all or substantially all (90% or more) of the fair market value of all the issued and outstanding shares of its capital stock are owned by one or more eligible Canadian public corporations that satisfy the first branch. Consequently, wholly owned Canadian operating subsidiaries of domestically controlled TSX-listed corporations can now access the 35% refundable SR&ED ITC (sharing the consolidated group's $6,000,000 expenditure limit), whereas Canadian subsidiaries controlled by foreign public or private parents remain restricted to the 15% non-refundable rate.
2.3 Mathematical Phase-Out Formulas for the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit
A. Standard Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula for CCPCs (Subsection 127(10.2))

For a CCPC that does not file an election to use the gross revenue phase-out method, its annual SR&ED expenditure limit is governed by subsection 127(10.2) of the Act based on the combined taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under section 181.2 of the Act and section 8601 of the Regulations) of the CCPC and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year. For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to shrink on a straight-line basis once prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 and is reduced to nil at $75,000,000:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount (if any) by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000

Subject to a statutory ceiling of $6,000,000 (when prior-year taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less) and a floor of nil (when prior-year taxable capital is $75,000,000 or more), every $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the corporation's $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1. As a worked example, if a CCPC has prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of $20,000,000, its expenditure limit is reduced by $500,000 ($5,000,000 excess ÷ 10) to $5,500,000, permitting the CCPC to claim up to $1,925,000 ($5,500,000 × 35%) in 100% refundable federal ITCs on current expenditures.

Corporate tax auditors must pay close attention to the balance sheet mechanics of sections 181 and 181.2 when verifying a CCPC's prior-year taxable capital. Under section 181, taxable capital is computed from the non-consolidated GAAP balance sheet presented to shareholders (without using the equity method). Under section 181.2, a corporation's capital includes all issued share capital (common and preferred shares at the full gross amount raised), retained earnings, contributed and other surpluses, loans and advances to the corporation, promissory and convertible notes, and long-term debt outstanding for more than 365 days, reduced only by the corporation's accounting deficit (not its T2 tax loss carryforwards) and its investment allowance (representing eligible investments in shares or debt of other corporations, such as a foreign subsidiary, or partnership interests). Crucially, cash deposits and government securities do not qualify for the investment allowance and do not reduce taxable capital. Furthermore, Simple Agreements for Future Equity (SAFEs) are included in taxable capital either as equity/surplus (if classified in shareholders' equity) or as a loan/advance (if classified as a liability). Because the test looks back to the immediately preceding taxation year, closing a large preferred-share financing round one day before fiscal year-end will swell that year-end balance sheet and grind down the following taxation year's SR&ED expenditure limit—unless the CCPC elects into the gross revenue phase-out formula. Practitioners must also note that the federal Small Business Deduction ($500,000 business limit under section 125) still phases out along the older $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 taxable capital corridor under subsection 125(5.1), and filing Schedule 33 remains mandatory whenever taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $10,000,000.
B. Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out Formula for ECPCs and Electing CCPCs (Subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.31), and 127(10.32))

For all Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and for any stand-alone CCPC (electing under subsection 127(10.31)) or associated group of CCPCs (making a mandatory joint election under subsection 127(10.32) via prescribed form), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is calculated under subsection 127(10.6) using the average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years, as reported in the consolidated financial statements of the corporation or consolidated group (with reasonable adjustments to eliminate intra-group sales of goods or services so that group revenue reflects a single economic entity):

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − B) ÷ $60,000,000, where B is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount (if any) by which average annual gross revenue for the three preceding fiscal years exceeds $15,000,000

Under subsection 127(10.64), if the corporation or group has fewer than three preceding fiscal years, the average annual revenue is computed across the actual number of preceding fiscal years (one or two years), and any preceding fiscal year shorter than 51 weeks must be annualized by multiplying its revenue by 365 divided by the number of days in that short fiscal year. Similarly, if the current taxation year of a CCPC or ECPC is shorter than 51 weeks, its current-year expenditure limit must be prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365. Because a CCPC (or associated group) may make the subsection 127(10.31)/(10.32) revenue election on a year-by-year basis, capital-intensive biotechnology, hardware, and deep-tech startups that have raised over $15,000,000 in equity capital but generate less than $15,000,000 in three-year average gross revenue can elect the revenue method and retain the full $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit.
2.4 Qualifying Corporation Status, the Qualifying Income Limit, and 40% Refundability Above the Limit

Under section 127.1 of the Act, a CCPC's ability to receive a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures exceeding its $6,000,000 expenditure limit hinges on whether the CCPC satisfies the definition of a "qualifying corporation" in subsection 127.1(2). A CCPC is a qualifying corporation for a given taxation year if its taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (aggregated with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their last taxation years ending in the preceding calendar year) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit (QIL).

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Qualifying Income Limit starts at $500,000 and is reduced along the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital corridor according to the formula set out in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy:

where A equals nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000. (For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the denominator was $40,000,000 and the threshold was $10,000,000.)

This statutory mechanism produces a critical divergence for CCPCs spending more than their expenditure limit. If a CCPC's prior-year taxable income is less than or equal to its QIL, it is a Qualifying Corporation: it receives 100% refundability on its 35% enhanced ITC on current expenditures up to its expenditure limit (and 40% refundability on capital expenditures), plus 40% refundability on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures above its expenditure limit. Because a loss-making CCPC has $0 prior-year taxable income, it remains a Qualifying Corporation so long as its prior-year taxable capital is below $75,000,000; however, the moment its prior-year taxable capital reaches or exceeds $75,000,000, its QIL drops to $0, causing the CRA to classify even a loss-making CCPC as a non-qualifying corporation whose 15% basic ITCs are 0% refundable. Conversely, if a profitable CCPC has prior-year taxable income exceeding its QIL (e.g., $1,200,000 of prior-year taxable income) but its prior-year taxable capital is below $75,000,000 (because the federal taxable income phase-out of the expenditure limit was eliminated for taxation years ending after March 18, 2019), the CCPC is classified as a "CCPC other than a qualifying or excluded corporation": it still earns the 35% enhanced ITC (100% refundable on current expenditures; 40% refundable on capital expenditures) up to its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, but any 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 limit is 0% refundable.
2.5 Associated Corporations and Group Allocation Rules (Section 256 & Subsections 127(10.3)–(10.4))

Under subsection 127(10.3) of the Act, all corporations that are associated with one another in a taxation year under section 256 must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit and combine their prior-year taxable capital (or three-year average gross revenue) when calculating phase-out reductions. Corporations are associated under section 256 where one controls the other, where both are controlled by the same person or group of persons, or where specified cross-shareholding and family relationships exist. Crucially, under subsection 256(1.4), any person holding a contractual, equitable, immediate, future, absolute, or contingent right to acquire shares or control voting rights—explicitly encompassing employee stock options, warrants, SAFEs, and convertible notes—is deemed for association and control purposes to own those underlying shares immediately.

Associated CCPCs must allocate the shared expenditure limit annually by filing Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated May 29, 2026). Consolidated groups of ECPCs (and associated CCPCs electing the three-year average revenue method) are likewise required to allocate the single $6,000,000 expenditure limit among group members (maintaining working papers until the CRA's dedicated ECPC allocation schedule is released). Under subsection 127(10.4), if an associated group fails to file an allocation agreement within 30 days of a written request by the CRA, the Minister is authorized to allocate the expenditure limit among the corporations unilaterally.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Costing Methodologies, and Capital Rules
3.1 Eligible Salaries and Wages (Lines 300 to 315 of Form T661)
A. Directly Engaged Salaries in Canada and the 90% ASA Rule

Under paragraph 37(1)(a), clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B) of the Act, and paragraph 2900(2)(b) of the Regulations, the foundational SR&ED expenditure category is the salary or wages (defined in subsection 248(1) as employment income under subdivision a of Division B of Part I, reported on a T4 slip) paid to employees directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Whether an employee is "directly engaged" is a question of fact governed by the hands-on technical duties performed, not the employee's corporate title. Eligible directly engaged duties encompass hands-on experimentation and analysis, the eight categories of paragraph 248(1)(d) support work commensurate with and directly supporting eligible SR&ED, non-specialized shop-floor personnel operating machinery or feeding raw materials strictly for supervised experimental runs, first-line technical supervision of hands-on SR&ED staff, ongoing technological project planning, technical feasibility studies, and preparing internal technical documentation of SR&ED work.

Pursuant to the All or Substantially All (ASA) Rule, an employee who spends 90% or more of their total working time during the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada is deemed to spend 100% of their time on SR&ED, allowing 100% of their eligible salary or wages to be claimed on Line 300 (non-specified employees) or Line 305 (specified employees) of Form T661. Employees spending less than 90% of their time directly engaged in SR&ED are claimed strictly in proportion to the actual hours or percentage of time spent directly on SR&ED. Under section 13.0 of the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, claimants must substantiate labour allocations across three evidentiary tiers—corporate/strategic level, project level, and activity level—using contemporaneous timesheets, project logs, supervisor summaries, and operational records.

Several categories of compensation are statutorily excluded from directly engaged SR&ED salary or wages under the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025). Employee stock option benefits (for options granted or shares issued on or after November 17, 2005), retiring allowances, payouts of extended vacation or sick leave, shareholder dividends, and sole proprietorship or partnership drawings are completely excluded. Furthermore, the employer's share of related benefits—including employer contributions to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Quebec Pension Plan (QPP), Employment Insurance (EI), provincial workers' compensation boards (WSIB in Ontario; CNESST in Quebec), approved employee pension plans, and medical/dental/optical insurance plans—cannot be claimed as directly engaged salaries on Lines 300–309; under the Proxy Method they are subsumed within the 55% PPA, whereas under the Traditional Method they are claimed as SR&ED overhead on Line 360. Finally, under subsection 248(16) of the Act, any GST/HST input tax credit or provincial sales tax rebate claimed by the employer on non-cash employee taxable benefits is deemed to be government assistance and must be stripped out of SR&ED salary claims.
B. The 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4) & Subsection 127(26))

Under subsection 78(4) of the Act, any salary, wages, or enforceable bonus incurred in a taxation year that is not paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year. Such unpaid remuneration must be identified on Line 315 of Form T661 and excluded from both the Section 37 pool and the Section 127 ITC calculation for that year; it becomes claimable on Line 310 of Form T661 only in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid. Conversely, for current SR&ED expenditures other than salary or wages (such as subcontractor invoices or materials), subsection 127(26) provides that amounts unpaid 180 days after year-end remain deductible in the Section 37 pool in the year incurred, but are excluded from Section 127 qualified expenditures on Line 520 of Form T661 until the taxation year in which they are paid.
C. Permissible Foreign Salaries: The 10% Outside-Canada Rule (Subsections 37(1.4) & 37(1.5))

Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the Act (reported on Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661), a claimant may include a restricted amount of "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED work performed outside Canada only if four cumulative conditions are satisfied:

items: The work outside Canada must be performed directly by an employee who is resident in Canada (payments to foreign or Canadian contractors/subcontractors for SR&ED performed outside Canada are 0% eligible without exception);
The work performed outside Canada must be an integral part of, and solely in support of, an SR&ED project carried on in Canada by the claimant;
The salary or wages paid for the work outside Canada must not be subject to an income or profits tax imposed by another country; and

The total foreign SR&ED salary or wages claimed for the taxation year cannot exceed 10% of the total eligible SR&ED salaries and wages incurred for SR&ED performed in Canada during that taxation year (10% of Line 306 on Form T661).

body.text: D. Specified Employee Restrictions and 2024–2026 YMPE Caps (Subsections 37(9), 37(9.1) & ITR 2900(7)–(8))

Stringent statutory limitations apply to any "specified employee," defined in subsection 248(1) of the Act as an employee who is a "specified shareholder" (a person who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer corporation or any related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, child, sibling, or parent of a controlling shareholder).

First, under subsection 37(9) of the Act, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits paid to a specified employee are completely excluded from SR&ED salary calculations. Second, for the purposes of the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and direct Section 127 qualified expenditures on Line 305 of Form T661, a specified employee's maximum claimable SR&ED salary (after multiplying by the percentage of time spent on SR&ED, with the 90% ASA rule still applicable on Line 305) is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee. Where a specified employee performs SR&ED for two or more associated corporations, this 5 × YMPE limit must be allocated among the associated group using Form T1174.

Third, when the claimant elects the Proxy Method, subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Regulations impose an even tighter dual ceiling on the amount of a specified employee's salary that may enter the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary base in Part 5 (Lines 850–860) of Form T661. In Part 5, the percentage of time a specified employee can be claimed as directly engaged in SR&ED (Box 854) is capped at a maximum of 75% (even if the founder/shareholder spent 100% of their working hours on hands-on SR&ED), and the resulting amount (Box 856) is further capped at Box 858, which equals 2.5 times the YMPE prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year:
Box 858 = 2.5 × YMPE × (number of days in the taxation year that the individual was employed by the claimant ÷ 365)

If the specified employee is also employed by an associated corporation, Box 858 cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE minus the amount included by the associated corporation in its PPA salary base for its taxation year ending in the same calendar year. Note that SR&ED caps are strictly governed by the base YMPE (First Earnings Ceiling), not the higher Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE / CPP2 Second Earnings Ceiling) introduced in 2024.

body.text: 3.2 Overhead Costing Methodologies: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

Every SR&ED claimant must make an annual, irrevocable election on Part 3 of Form T661 (ticking Line 160 for the Proxy Method or Line 162 for the Traditional Method) when filing its initial SR&ED claim for the taxation year. If the claimant does not explicitly elect the Proxy Method on Line 160 upon initial filing, the Traditional Method applies automatically and cannot be changed for that taxation year.
A. The Proxy Method and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (ITR 2900(4) & 2900(6))

Under the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Act and subsection 2900(4) of the Regulations), the claimant does not specifically identify or track actual SR&ED overhead costs. Instead, the claimant computes a notional overhead amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base (Line 818 × 55% = Line 820 / Line 502). (While the PPA rate was 65% prior to 2013 and 60% in 2013, it has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 2014; using 65% on a contemporary return is a frequent compliance error that results in immediate reassessment.)

Because the PPA is a notional figure rather than an actual cash expenditure, it is included solely in the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (Line 502) to generate SR&ED ITCs; neither the PPA nor the actual overhead expenditures it represents can be added to the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool (actual overhead costs are instead deducted as ordinary business expenses under Section 9 of the Act). Furthermore, subsection 2900(6) of the Regulations subjects the PPA to an Overall Cap designed to ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specified statutory deductions do not exceed the business's total tax deductions for the year:
PPA ≤ A − B − C

In this formula, A represents total deductions claimed in computing net business income for the year (including cost of goods sold); B represents the sum of specific statutory deductions claimed under sections 20 (such as CCA, interest, and bad debts), 24 (ceasing business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (SR&ED pool deductions), 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development), and 104 (trusts) of the Act; and C represents expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (rent). Provided a claimant deducts more than $55 of non-SR&ED, non-building operating expenses for every $100 of eligible salary in the salary base, the Overall Cap does not restrict the 55% PPA.

A critical audit issue in the software, data analytics, and artificial intelligence industries involves cloud computing and SaaS subscriptions (such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, or CAD software subscriptions). Under the Proxy Method, actual overhead and support infrastructure costs are completely replaced by the 55% PPA; because cloud computing and software subscriptions are neither tangible "materials consumed or transformed" nor "SR&ED contracts" performed on the claimant's behalf, cloud computing and subscription costs cannot be claimed separately under the Proxy Method. Only if a compute-intensive company's incremental SR&ED cloud computing expenses and other directly related overheads exceed 55% of its SR&ED salary base should it elect the Traditional Method on Line 162 and claim those tracked, incremental cloud costs on Line 360.
B. The Traditional Method (ITR 2900(2)(c) & 2900(3))

Under the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the Act and paragraphs 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3) of the Regulations), the claimant foregoes the 55% PPA and instead identifies, tracks, and substantiates actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. Unlike the notional PPA, actual overhead expenditures claimed under the Traditional Method are added to both the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes.

To qualify on Line 360 under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022), each expenditure must be either all or substantially all (≥90%) attributable to SR&ED in Canada or directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (meaning the cost is connected directly to SR&ED work, staff, or equipment without intervening steps, and would not have been incurred but for the SR&ED). Eligible Traditional Method overheads on Line 360 include the employer's share of related benefits (CPP/QPP, EI, WSIB/CNESST, pension, and group medical/dental insurance) for hands-on SR&ED employees; salaries and wages of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support SR&ED (other than hands-on directly engaged staff), as well as clerical and administrative staff salaries where there is a direct linkage to SR&ED and the cost is incremental (note that related benefits, retiring allowances, training, and travel for clerical and administrative staff are disallowed as indirect linkages); moving and recruitment expenses for SR&ED personnel; incremental utilities, lab supplies, and proportional maintenance/upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment (excluding fixed-cost maintenance contracts, lawn/garden care, and post-project waste disposal); and post-December 15, 2024 lease costs for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time.
3.3 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant engages an arm's-length Canadian resident contractor to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf (where the payer controls the work and owns the resulting intellectual property), 100% of the contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool on Line 340 of Form T661. However, for Section 127 ITC purposes, Line 529 of Form T661 deducts 20% of the contract amount pursuant to subsection 127(9) of the Act, so only 80% of arm's-length SR&ED contract expenditures qualify for the SR&ED ITC. Under subsection 127(24), the contractor must be a taxable Canadian supplier (or perform the work through a Canadian permanent establishment), and any portion of the contract work subcontracted outside Canada is completely ineligible.

By contrast, expenditures for SR&ED performed on a claimant's behalf by a non-arm's-length (NAL) party (reported on Line 345) are 0% eligible for the payer's ITC and must be deducted in full on Line 541 of Form T661. To transfer the tax credit benefit to the payer, the NAL performer ("transferor") and the payer ("transferee") must jointly execute and file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) under subsections 127(13) to (16) of the Act, allowing the performer to transfer its underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures (including its 55% PPA, capped at the contract amount) to the payer on Line 508. Where a claimant purchases non-SR&ED goods or services from a NAL supplier, subsections 127(11.6) to (11.8) limit the qualified expenditure to the NAL supplier's adjusted selling cost or adjusted service cost, eliminating intercompany profit on Line 542.

Additionally, under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) of the Act and the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy, a claimant may make third-party payments (reported on Form T1263 and Line 370 of Form T661) to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, approved associations, granting councils, or tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations (classified as Entities A through F) for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to the claimant's business, provided the claimant is entitled to exploit the results on a non-exclusive basis. Like arm's-length contracts, third-party payments on Line 370 are reduced by 20% on Line 529, so 80% qualifies for the Section 127 ITC. Payments to Entities B through F earn ITCs on a cash basis in the year paid, whereas payments to Entity A (Canadian resident corporations) earn ITCs on an accrual basis as the SR&ED is performed.
3.4 Materials Consumed or Transformed and Production Runs (Lines 320 & 325)

Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the Act, and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations, claimants under either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method may claim 100% of the laid-down cost (including invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation/freight, and storage costs) of materials that compose the physical body of a thing on which SR&ED is performed in Canada. Materials Consumed (Line 320) are materials absorbed, broken down, destroyed, or rendered virtually valueless (retaining less than 10% of their original cost) during SR&ED; if 90% or more (ASA) of a material's cost is consumed in SR&ED, 100% of its cost is claimable. Under the Materials for SR&ED Policy, direct energy inputs in endothermic chemical, metallurgical, glass, or ceramic processes where the product physically retains the energy, as well as process water that chemically enters an experimental product and is rendered useless, also qualify as materials consumed. Materials Transformed (Line 325) are materials incorporated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or trial batch that retains some commercial or scrap value (10% or more of original cost) to the claimant or another party, claimed in the taxation year in which transformation occurs.

When experimental development takes place on a manufacturing shop floor or in a commercial plant, the CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy and SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy distinguish between two operational contexts:

items: Experimental Development Resulting in Experimental Production (ED+EP): Applies where experimental parameters are pushed outside established operating ranges and create genuine technical risk of process instability, equipment damage, yield loss, or unsaleable output (including dedicated non-commercial pilot plants). In an ED+EP run, 100% of the direct labour and materials consumed or transformed in producing the required experimental production batch are allowable SR&ED expenditures (excluding any excess commercial production).

Experimental Development Simultaneous with Commercial Production (ED+CP): Applies where experimental tests occur alongside normal commercial production runs without technical risk to the baseline run. In an ED+CP run, standard commercial labour and input materials are excluded; only the incremental labour and material costs incurred over and above normal commercial production qualify as SR&ED. Similarly, when developing a custom commercial asset where separating SR&ED costs from commercial construction costs is exceptionally difficult, the CRA permits an "alternative approach" under which allowable SR&ED expenditures equal the total actual cost of developing the asset minus the estimated cost of constructing the asset had the technology already existed, plus incremental SR&ED costs.

body.text: 3.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Lease Costs, and Recapture (Post-December 15, 2024)
A. Full Capital Expenditures: The 90% ASA Intent Test and Used Property Restriction

By re-enacting paragraph 37(1)(b) and amending subsections 37(6), 37(8), 127(9), and 127.1(2.01) of the Act, Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired (and available for use) on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024). Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (published June 29, 2026) and Form T661 (26) (Lines 262, 263, and 390), a capital expenditure to acquire depreciable property owned by the claimant qualifies on Line 390 if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant establishes the intent (supported by project plans, business cases, or capital requests) to either: (1) use the property during all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada; or (2) consume all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its value in performing SR&ED in Canada (such as specialized laboratory apparatus, prototyping tooling, or AI compute hardware whose economic value is exhausted during the SR&ED project).
Four critical statutory rules govern restored SR&ED capital expenditures:

items: Immediate 100% Section 37 Deduction (Deemed CCA): Eligible capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 enter the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool (allowing 100% immediate expensing in the year the property becomes available for use), and any amount deducted under subsection 37(1) is deemed by subsection 37(6) to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed on the property.

Used Property Excluded from Section 127 ITC (Line 532): While both new and used depreciable property meeting the 90% ASA test can be deducted in the Section 37 pool, used property (property that was used, or acquired for use or lease, for any purpose before it was acquired by the claimant) is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902 and is ineligible for the Section 127 ITC; used capital property must be deducted on Line 532 of Form T661.

Exclusion of Land and Buildings vs. Inclusion of Software Tools: Land is non-depreciable and never qualifies. Under paragraph 37(8)(e) of the Act, buildings and leasehold interests in buildings are excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures, except for a prescribed special-purpose building under Section 2903 of the Regulations. Conversely, under section 5 of the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), systems software and enduring software licences (lasting beyond one fiscal year) acquired after December 15, 2024, as a tool to perform SR&ED (and not incorporated into a commercial product) qualify as SR&ED capital expenditures.

40% Refundability Ceiling on Capital ITCs: Pursuant to subsection 127.1(2.01) of the Act, for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earning the 35% enhanced ITC within their $6,000,000 expenditure limit, ITCs earned on capital expenditures (and capital lease costs) are 40% refundable (providing an immediate 14% cash refund and a 21% non-refundable ITC carryforward on eligible new capital acquisitions).

body.text: B. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Line 504) and Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP)

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (published May 22, 2026) and subsection 127(9) of the Act, new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the 90% ASA useful-life test may still qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661 (under both the Proxy and Traditional Methods) if it is used primarily (more than 50% of its actual operating time) for SR&ED in Canada, is not General-Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the Regulations (property intended at acquisition both for SR&ED during the assembly/commissioning of a commercial facility and for primary non-SR&ED use over its expected useful life).

If the new equipment is used >50% of its operating time for SR&ED in the First Period (from the date it becomes available for use to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition), 25% of its capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC as First-Term SUE on Line 504. If it qualified as First-Term SUE and continues to be used >50% of its operating time for SR&ED in the Second Period (ending at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition), an additional 25% of its capital cost (totalling 50%) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC as Second-Term SUE on Line 504. Unlike 90% ASA capital property on Line 390, the capital cost of SUE does not enter the Section 37 deductible SR&ED pool and is instead depreciated under normal CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8.
C. Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Official CRA T661 guidance, the CRA's updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (published June 8, 2026), and the Department of Finance explanatory notes to sections 37, 127, and 127.1 confirm that equipment lease payments first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024, for depreciable equipment used in SR&ED qualify for SR&ED incentives. Specifically, if leased equipment (excluding GPOEF under the Proxy Method) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time in SR&ED in Canada, the lease cost qualifies as an SR&ED expenditure of a capital nature under both methods. If the leased equipment is used less than 90% of its operating time in SR&ED, no lease cost is claimable under the Proxy Method, whereas under the Traditional Method the proportional SR&ED operating percentage of the lease cost incurred after December 15, 2024, may be claimed on Line 360 as an overhead expenditure.
D. Recapture of SR&ED ITCs and CCA (Subsections 127(27) to (36) & Line 440)

Under subsections 127(27) to (36) of the Act and the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, selling or converting to commercial use any property—materials transformed (Line 325), ASA capital property (Line 390), or Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504)—for which an SR&ED ITC was claimed within the preceding 20 taxation years triggers SR&ED ITC Recapture. The recaptured amount equals the lesser of the original ITC earned on the property or the original ITC rate (35% or 15%) multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value on commercial conversion or non-arm's-length transfer; for SUE, applied to 25% or 50% of the proceeds/FMV). Recaptured ITCs are added directly to Part I tax payable in the year of disposition/conversion (creating a tax liability even in a loss year unless offset by unused ITCs) and simultaneously increase the taxpayer's Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the following taxation year on Line 453 of Form T661. For ASA capital property deducted in the Section 37 pool, Line 440 of Form T661 reduces the Section 37 pool by the lesser of the proceeds of disposition and the undeducted pool balance, while any excess proceeds up to original cost trigger CCA Recapture in taxable income on Schedule T2SCH1.
4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Stacking Mechanics
4.1 Government Assistance Mechanics and Iterative Federal-Provincial Stacking

Pursuant to subsection 127(9) and paragraph 127(11.1)(c) of the federal Income Tax Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits—along with direct government grants, subsidies, and forgivable loans such as the National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP)—constitute "government assistance". Any government assistance that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its filing-due date in respect of SR&ED must be deducted on Lines 429 and 513–517 of Form T661, reducing both the Section 37 deductible SR&ED pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool for federal ITC purposes. (Note that in-kind technical advisory support does not constitute government assistance, and bona fide public loans made after 2019 that qualify as "excluded loans" under subsection 12(11) are exempt from government assistance treatment under Bill C-69.)

Crucially, under the Proxy Method, provincial R&D tax credits and direct wage grants (such as NRC IRAP or CEWS) do not reduce the Part 5 salary base used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Instead, the 55% PPA is calculated on the unreduced eligible SR&ED salary base first, added to direct SR&ED expenditures to establish gross qualified expenditures, and then reduced by the provincial tax credit and grant assistance in Part 4 of Form T661.

To illustrate this interaction in concrete dollar terms, consider a qualifying CCPC (within its full expenditure limit) that incurs $1,000,000 of eligible directly engaged non-specified SR&ED salaries in 2026 and elects the Proxy Method, generating a $550,000 PPA and $1,550,000 of pre-assistance qualified expenditures:

items: In British Columbia (10% Refundable BC SR&ED Credit): The corporation claims a 10% BC SR&ED credit on the $1,550,000 qualified expenditure base, yielding $155,000 in refundable provincial credits. That $155,000 provincial credit reduces the federal qualified expenditure pool from $1,550,000 to $1,395,000, which earns a 35% federal enhanced ITC of $488,250. The combined cash refund is $643,250 ($155,000 BC + $488,250 federal), representing 64.325% of the $1,000,000 cash salary outlay (or 41.5% of the $1,550,000 proxy-loaded expenditure base).

In Ontario (8% Refundable OITC + 3.5% Non-Refundable ORDTC): The corporation claims an 8% OITC on the $1,550,000 qualified expenditure base, yielding $124,000 in refundable Ontario credits. If the CCPC is in a tax loss position and waives the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), its federal qualified expenditure pool is reduced only by the $124,000 OITC to $1,426,000, earning $499,100 ($1,426,000 × 35%) in refundable federal ITCs for a combined cash refund of $623,100 (62.31% of cash salary; 40.2% of proxy-loaded base). If the CCPC instead claims the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC on the OITC-reduced base ($1,426,000 × 3.5% = $49,910 non-refundable ORDTC), its federal pool is further ground down to $1,376,090, earning $481,631.50 in refundable federal ITCs (reducing immediate cash refunds by $17,468.50 in exchange for $49,910 of non-refundable Ontario credit carryforwards).

In Quebec (New 30% Refundable CRIC Regime): Under Quebec's post-March 25, 2025 CRIC (which applies to actual Quebec R&D salaries without a proxy, above an exclusion threshold of at least $50,000), $1,000,000 of salary minus the $50,000 threshold leaves $950,000 of eligible Quebec expenditures, earning a 30% refundable CRIC of $285,000. Deducting that $285,000 provincial credit from the federal proxy-loaded pool ($1,550,000 − $285,000 = $1,265,000) generates a 35% refundable federal ITC of $442,750, yielding a combined cash refund of $727,750 (72.775% of the $1,000,000 cash salary outlay).

body.text: 4.3 Deep-Dive Analysis of Key Provincial Jurisdictions
A. Quebec's Transition to the CRIC Regime (March 25, 2025)

For taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, the Gouvernement du Québec replaced its four legacy R&D tax credits (Salaries and Wages on Form RD-1029.7-V; University/Public Research Centre on Form RD-1029.8.6-V; Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research on Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V; and Research Consortium Fees/Dues on Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, noting that cumulative consortium fees paid in a year beginning before March 26, 2025, retain transitional carryforward eligibility until December 31, 2029) with the single, unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T and Form RD-222-V.

While Quebec legislation remains harmonized with federal subsection 248(1) for the core definition of R&D (and the CRA continues to perform the scientific review of R&D activities), the CRIC broadens provincial eligibility to include pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Quebec in conjunction with R&D carried out in Quebec by or on behalf of the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialization activities include: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to satisfy regulatory requirements and obtain an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation; and (2) product design, including developing form and aesthetics, improving functionality, and selecting materials.

The CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit to all eligible corporations operating a business with an establishment in Quebec (including large public and foreign-controlled corporations) at a rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the annual exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 tier. Qualified CRIC expenditures encompass 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for Quebec R&D or pre-commercialization work, 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for contracts carried out in Quebec, 50% of payments made to eligible public research centres, research consortia, or university entities, and 100% of capital property acquisition costs for depreciable property used in Quebec R&D or pre-commercialization (excluding land, buildings, rights to use land or buildings, and property used under a Large Investment Project qualification certificate). Each taxation year, qualified expenditures must first exceed an applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the personal income tax basic personal amount for each employee adjusted for the proportion of time spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities.
B. Ontario's Tri-Partite Regime (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario may access three distinct credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule 566) provides an 8% fully refundable credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (up to $240,000 per year). Crucially, Ontario did not mirror federal Bill C-15: the OITC expenditure limit remains $3,000,000 (not $6,000,000), eligibility remains restricted exclusively to CCPCs (excluding ECPCs), and the $3,000,000 limit phases out linearly when prior-year associated taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or when prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Section 38, Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit (with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward) to all corporations on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures reduced by any OITC and OBRITC claimed. Because any ORDTC claimed is treated as government assistance that reduces the federal 35% refundable SR&ED pool, corporations that cannot immediately utilize non-refundable Ontario credits may elect to waive the ORDTC in whole or in part under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario). Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Schedules 568 & 569) provides a 20% fully refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 of qualified expenditures incurred under eligible contracts with qualifying Ontario research institutes (up to $4,000,000 in annual refundable credits per associated group).
C. British Columbia (Budget 2026 Reforms), Alberta (IEG), and Saskatchewan

In British Columbia, Budget 2026 enacted three major structural upgrades to the 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit (claimed on Form T666 within 18 months of taxation year-end under Part 6 of the British Columbia Income Tax Act): (1) it eliminated the statutory sunset clause (previously September 1, 2027), making the BC credit permanent; (2) it harmonized the provincial refundable expenditure limit with the federal $6,000,000 limit (generating up to $600,000 in refundable BC credits per year, phased out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000) and restored capital expenditure eligibility for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024; and (3) it extended 100% refundability up to the expenditure limit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside CCPCs. Non-refundable BC SR&ED credits (earned above the expenditure limit or by non-CCPC/non-ECPC corporations) may be carried back 3 years or carried forward 10 taxation years, and BC enforces a 10-year recapture window under sections 102.1 to 102.6.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)—administered separately by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and claimed on Form AT1 Schedule 29 within 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing-due date (21 months after year-end)—provides a 100% refundable credit on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta SR&ED expenditures. The IEG pays 8% on Alberta SR&ED spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (the average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years) and an enhanced 20% on incremental spending above that two-year average, phasing out linearly between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital. In Saskatchewan, the 10% Saskatchewan R&D Tax Credit is claimed on Schedule 403 with the T2 return under section 63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000; for qualifying expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024, Saskatchewan doubled the 10% refundable CCPC threshold from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 of qualifying expenditures per year (yielding up to $200,000 in refundable credits), while expenditures above $2,000,000 (and all expenditures of non-CCPCs) earn a 10% non-refundable credit, subject to a combined annual ceiling of $1,000,000 in total credits ($10,000,000 of spending) per corporation.
5. Administrative Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, Prescribed Forms, Deadlines, and Penalties
5.1 The Statutory 18-Month Reporting Deadline (Subsections 37(11), 127(9)(m), & 220(2.2))

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must file Form T661 containing the prescribed project and financial information, along with Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals), on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date under section 150 for the taxation year. Because a corporation's T2 filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after its taxation year-end, the absolute statutory SR&ED reporting deadline for a corporation is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, June 30, 2026, for a December 31, 2024 taxation year-end). For an unincorporated individual carrying on a business, the T1 filing-due date is June 15 of the following year, making the SR&ED reporting deadline June 15 of the second following calendar year (17.5 months after the December 31 year-end).

Pursuant to subsection 220(2.2) of the Act, the CRA has zero statutory discretion under subsection 220(2.1) or the taxpayer relief rules in subsection 220(3.1) to waive or extend the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline. As affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. Canada, 2016 FCA 301, failing to file the prescribed forms with the prescribed information by the 18-month deadline (unless the deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday, in which case it shifts to the next business day) permanently bars the SR&ED claim. Under the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025), if a claimant files Form T661 on time for 15 projects but omits Part 2 project descriptions for 5 of those projects, the CRA will allow the 10 complete projects and disallow the 5 incomplete projects once the 18-month deadline expires. (Where a claimant has more than 20 SR&ED projects in a year, Part 2 of Form T661 permits filing the project descriptions for the 20 largest projects in dollar value with the return, provided the remaining project descriptions are retained on file and produced upon CRA request.) Note also that deducting previously pooled amounts from the Section 37 expenditure pool in future years is not subject to the 18-month deadline, provided the underlying expenditures were reported on Form T661 on time in the year incurred.
5.2 The New Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process announced in Federal Budget 2025. Through a streamlined application submitted via My Business Account (with optional one-on-one pre-application support available from the CRA at OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca), eligible businesses can request a formal up-front determination of whether their planned R&D projects satisfy the scientific/technological eligibility requirements of subsection 248(1) before starting work or incurring expenditures.

The CRA's service standard for issuing a Pre-Claim Approval determination is eight (8) weeks. When the claimant subsequently files Form T661 (26) after completing the work, it ticks Line 212 and enters its Pre-Claim Approval Case Number on Line 214. Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated October 29, 2025 / April 20, 2026), claims containing pre-approved projects are normally selected for an expenditure-only review and processed within an accelerated service standard of 90 calendar days (compared to 180 calendar days for standard refundable SR&ED claims selected for technical and financial review, and 60 calendar days for refundable claims processed without review). Only if the executed work diverged significantly from the pre-approved project scope, or if non-pre-approved projects are bundled into the claim, will the CRA conduct a full post-filing technical review under the standard 180-day timeline.

On May 15, 2026, the CRA issued the revised Form T661 (26) (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), followed by revised Schedule T2SCH31 (May 22, 2026) and Schedule T2SCH49 (May 29, 2026), incorporating the Bill C-15 and Pre-Claim Approval changes.
