body.text: 5.4 Claim Preparer Penalties (Subsections 162(5.1)–(5.2)) and Gross Negligence Penalties (Subsection 163(2))

Under subsection 162(5.1) of the Act, if any required information in Part 9 of Form T661 (disclosing every external claim preparer, their Business Number, contingency or hourly billing structure, and fee amount) is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed in respect of each SR&ED claim. Where a claim preparer knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence makes or participates in a false statement or omission in Part 9, subsection 162(5.2) holds the claimant and the claim preparer jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable for the $1,000 penalty. Per the CRA's January 28, 2025 revision to the SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, Part 9 information is not subject to the 18-month reporting deadline disallowance rule, meaning an omission in Part 9 triggers the $1,000 penalty and processing delays rather than disqualifying the underlying SR&ED claim.

Furthermore, under subsection 163(2) of the Act and the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), any taxpayer who knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission in an SR&ED claim (including an amended return) is subject to a civil penalty equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the understated Part I tax payable and/or overstated refundable ITC claimed. The CRA bears the burden of proving gross negligence on a balance of probabilities (showing more than simple oversight or misunderstanding). Under the statutory ordering rule, overstated SR&ED expenditures are treated as deducted first, and the 50% penalty applies to the combined tax understatement resulting from both the overstated Section 37 deduction and the overstated Section 127 ITC. Once an SR&ED claim is selected for review, the claimant cannot withdraw the claim; Form T661 forms part of the tax return and the Part 10 certification cannot be revoked.
5.5 Dispute Resolution: Three-Step Administrative Review (Form RC532) and Formal Appeals

Under the CRA's Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns (updated December 5, 2025) and The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), technical reviews by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and financial reviews by a Financial Reviewer (FR) are conducted primarily via virtual videoconferencing (with on-site visits granted on an exceptional case-by-case basis), and claimants may also inspect the CV of any outside technical consultant engaged by the CRA under Application Policy SR&ED 95-04R to guard against conflicts of interest. If a disagreement arises during a review, the CRA provides a sequential three-step resolution mechanism prior to file closure:

items: Step One — Direct Discussion with the RTA and/or FR: The claimant presents additional contemporaneous documentation and technical clarifications directly to the assigned RTA and/or FR in response to their preliminary findings.

Step Two — Escalation to Management (RTM / FRM): If the disagreement remains unresolved, the claimant escalates the matter to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM), who review the case facts and perspectives of both parties.

Step Three — Request for Administrative Review (Form RC532): After receiving the CRA's formal 30-day proposal package and before the file is closed, the claimant may submit Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Business Tax Incentives Directorate, Enterprise Building, 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa ON K1A 0L5), which forwards the request within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director. An Administrative Review is not a second technical audit; the Assistant Director evaluates strictly whether due process was provided and whether the review conclusions complied with current SR&ED legislation and CRA policies.

body.text: Once a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, a claimant that disagrees with the outcome may file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch within 90 days, and subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal. Under subsection 230(4)(b) of the Act, all books, financial records, and contemporaneous SR&ED documentation must be retained for a minimum of six (6) years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate.
6. Judicial Precedents, Audit Standards, and Case Law Analysis (1997–2026)
6.1 The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic, Consoltex, RIS-Christie, and C.W. Agencies

The cornerstone of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence is Chief Justice Bowman's decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC). Reaffirming his earlier pronouncement in Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, (1997), 97 D.T.C. 724 (TCC) and applying Section 12 of the Interpretation Act, Chief Justice Bowman held (at para. 11) that because Parliament enacted the SR&ED tax incentives to encourage scientific research in Canada, courts and tax authorities must give the SR&ED provisions a "fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its objects".

At paragraph 16 of Northwest Hydraulic—subsequently approved and adopted as the binding national legal standard by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (at para. 17)—Chief Justice Bowman formulated the Five Questions (or Five Criteria) that a taxpayer must establish on a balance of probabilities to prove that an activity constitutes SR&ED:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? ("Routine engineering" refers to techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field.)
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses?
Did the process result in a technological advancement?
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: 6.2 Evolution of Evidentiary, Methodological, and Expert Witness Standards (1998–2022)

Over the subsequent two decades, the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal clarified the evidentiary application of each of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria. First, in 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 560 (TCC), Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313 (2014 CCI 313) (per Jorré J. at para. 94), and Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42 (at para. 118), the Tax Court held that while subsection 248(1) does not make a rigid documentary format an absolute statutory precondition for SR&ED eligibility, contemporaneous documentation is practically essential to establish disputed facts and prove that systematic experimentation occurred. In Les Abeilles, the Tax Court also confirmed that the need to develop a cost-effective manufacturing or packaging solution can constitute genuine technological uncertainty if existing industry solutions are commercially or technically impractical in the claimant's context.

Second, in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355, the courts dismissed SR&ED claims involving thermoforming and injection moulding of storage bins because the work relied on well-known manufacturing techniques and routine engineering rather than resolving a technological uncertainty. Similarly, in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, Justice Sommerfeldt defined a "hypothesis" (at para. 26) as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial" and distilled the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion (the scientific method, at para. 33) into three essential characteristics: (1) trained and systematic observation, (2) measurement and experiment, and (3) formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses.

Third, in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47), the Federal Court of Appeal rejected arguments by taxpayers that the absence of the phrase "scientific method" in subsection 248(1)—or the CRA's August 2021 publication of its "Why and How" eligibility guidelines—eliminated the requirement to follow the scientific method under the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria. The Federal Court of Appeal emphasized that it is the exclusive role of the courts to interpret the Income Tax Act and that the Northwest Hydraulic test remains binding law, applied flexibly to fit the taxpayer's applied science or business environment. Furthermore, National R&D warned litigants that an expert witness report will be ruled inadmissible if the expert purports to answer the ultimate legal question before the court (whether the work constitutes SR&ED) rather than providing technical evidence on the underlying state of science or technology.
6.3 Recent Landmark Rulings (2024–2026): Manning Canning and Tuna Temple
Two recent decisions—one from the Tax Court of Canada in December 2024 / January 2025 and one from the Federal Court of Appeal in October 2026—define the current litigation boundary for SR&ED claims:

In Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 159 (Original Judgment: December 13, 2024; Amended Reasons: January 17, 2025, per Bodie J.), a Toronto food and beverage company claimed SR&ED in its 2020 taxation year for developing "Chrisoda," an unpasteurized vinegar-based beverage made with cold-pressed fruit juice packaged in cans and shelf-stable at room temperature for at least two years. Because cold-pressed juice contains natural microbes that caused early canned batches to ferment and explode, and because standard chemical preservatives (potassium sorbate and sodium benzoate) ruined the taste and clarity, Manning Canning worked with an external food scientist to formulate and test hypotheses using Chiber, a natural white button mushroom extract that had previously only ever been used in dairy products. By systematically varying and measuring juice concentrate, water, carbonation, Brix (sugar content), and pH across sequential experimental trials, the company achieved room-temperature stability. Allowing the taxpayer's appeal, Justice Bodie established three major principles: (1) technological uncertainty can exist even when using a publicly available compound or solution (Chiber), provided that solution has never been applied in the specific technical context or environment at issue; (2) contemporaneous documentation is meant to track hypotheses, experiments, and results for the performer's own progression and does not need to be written for an outsider unfamiliar with the field to replicate the results; and (3) the five Northwest Hydraulic questions remain the valid, governing judicial methodology notwithstanding the CRA's administrative "Why and How" guidelines.

Conversely, in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175 (decided October 20–21, 2026; affirming 2025 TCC 183), the taxpayer claimed SR&ED deductions and ITCs for 14 fish-cutting and recipe projects across its 2005 to 2009 taxation years. The Minister disallowed 13 of the 14 projects, and the Tax Court upheld the reassessments because the projects lacked hypotheses, used existing technology and trial-and-error methods, had inadequate records, and failed to establish a gap in industry knowledge. On appeal, the taxpayer argued that the Tax Court erred because it had found the taxpayer's witness to be credible, cross-examination had not displaced the testimony, and the Crown called no contradicting witness. Dismissing the appeal with costs, the Federal Court of Appeal established a critical appellate distinction between witness credibility and sufficiency of evidence: finding a witness honest and credible does not, by itself, establish a prima facie case that demolishes the Minister's factual assumptions when the substance of the testimony describes trial-and-error business improvements rather than an objective industry knowledge gap and adherence to the scientific method under the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria.

body.text: 7. Audit Verification Checklist for Canadian R&D Tax Claims (2026)

To ensure complete statutory compliance across federal and provincial R&D filings in Canada, tax auditors and corporate claimants should verify the following ten technical checkpoints prior to filing:

items: Verify Taxation Year Start Date vs. Asset Acquisition Date for Bill C-15 Rules: Confirm whether the corporation's taxation year began on or after December 16, 2024. Only taxation years starting on or after December 16, 2024, qualify for the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the $15,000,000–$75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out, ECPC eligibility, and the CCPC gross revenue election. Conversely, capital expenditures and lease costs are governed by an acquisition/payable date test and qualify on or after December 16, 2024, even if the taxation year began before December 16, 2024 (with operating time calculated for the period after December 15, 2024).

Model Both Taxable Capital and 3-Year Average Gross Revenue for CCPCs: For any CCPC (or associated group) whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000 (for instance, due to equity financing rounds held in cash on the year-end balance sheet), calculate the three-year average gross revenue test under subsections 127(10.31)/(10.32) and 127(10.6) and file the annual revenue election if it preserves a higher expenditure limit.

Audit Specified Employee Caps Against Exact Calendar-Year YMPE: Ensure all employees owning 10% or more of any class of shares and non-arm's-length relatives are reported as specified employees on Line 305 and Part 5 (Lines 850–860); exclude all bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits; and apply the exact calendar-year YMPE ($68,500 for 2024, $71,300 for 2025, and $74,600 for 2026) rather than the CPP2 YAMPE.

Enforce the 55% PPA Rate and Cloud Computing Rules: Confirm that Part 5 of Form T661 applies the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount rate under Regulation 2900(4), verify the Regulation 2900(6) Overall Cap, and ensure that cloud computing / SaaS subscriptions are never claimed as materials or contracts under the Proxy Method (or elect the Traditional Method on Line 162 if incremental SR&ED cloud compute and direct overheads exceed 55% of the salary base).

Segregate New vs. Used Capital Property and SUE: For post-December 15, 2024 capital acquisitions, verify documented 90% ASA intent over expected useful life for Line 390; back out any used depreciable property on Line 532 so it does not claim Section 127 ITCs; and ensure Shared-Use Equipment (>50% SR&ED operating time) is claimed at 25% per period on Line 504 while depreciating its capital cost on Schedule T2SCH8.

Verify Subcontractor Geography, NAL Transfers, and 180-Day Payment Cutoffs: Confirm that 100% of claimed subcontractor work was performed physically inside Canada; apply the 80% ITC inclusion rate (Line 529) to arm's-length contracts and third-party payments; execute Form T1146 before the transferor's filing-due date for any non-arm's-length SR&ED contract transfers; and exclude any salary or wages unpaid 180 days after year-end under subsection 78(4) (Line 315).

Review Post-2019 Public Loans Under Bill C-69: Inspect all government loans received since January 1, 2020, to determine whether they qualify as bona fide "excluded loans" under subsection 12(11) and subsection 127(9), and file amended returns for non-statute-barred years if such loans were previously deducted as government assistance.

Optimize Provincial Credits and Section 12(1)(t) / 37(1)(d) Interactions: Calculate provincial credits first—applying the new 30%/20% CRIC on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T in Quebec for tax years starting after March 25, 2025, the permanent 10% BC SR&ED credit up to $6,000,000 on Form T666, the 8% OITC up to $3,000,000 on Schedule 566 in Ontario (evaluating whether to waive the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC), the 8%/20% IEG on AT1 Schedule 29 in Alberta, and the expanded $2,000,000 refundable threshold on Schedule 403 in Saskatchewan—before deducting provincial government assistance on Form T661.

Complete New Form T661 (26) Lines and Part 9 Disclosures: Ensure Line 207 (5-digit CRDC Field of Research code RDF#####), Lines 212/214 (Pre-Claim Approval Case Number, if applicable), Lines 262/263 (top 10 capital assets and operating time percentages), and Part 9 (claim preparer details) are accurately completed to avoid the $1,000 penalty under subsection 162(5.1).

Map Contemporaneous Evidence to the Five Northwest Hydraulic Questions: In light of Manning Canning (2024 TCC 159) and Tuna Temple (2026 FCA 175), ensure that every project file contains dated, contemporaneous evidence demonstrating why the objective could not be achieved through routine engineering, explicitly stating the hypotheses formulated, logging quantitative experimental parameters and test results, and recording the resulting technological advancement.
